title: Linux, Unix and Windows: differences in day-to-day operations

videos.script: Right now, somewhere, a machine you will never see is answering a question you asked. It is almost certainly running Linux. {{scale}} Most of the web, most of the cloud, every Android phone, the computers inside your car and your television — Linux underneath. And the people who look after those machines do not click on them. They type. {{terminal}} That is what this course is: learning to talk to a computer in sentences instead of gestures. Here is the part nobody says at the start. The terminal is not a harder way to do what you already do with a mouse. It is a different deal, and you should know what you are trading. You give up discoverability — nothing is shown to you, nothing is labelled, there is no menu to go looking through. What you get back is precision, repetition and reach. You can do the same thing to ten thousand files. You can do it again next Tuesday without having to remember how. You can do it on a machine on another continent that has no screen attached to it at all. {{trade}} The first hour is uncomfortable. Everybody's first hour is uncomfortable, including the people who now do this for a living. By the end of this lesson you will know what you are actually looking at when a terminal opens, how to get a Linux of your own to practise on, and why a command that failed just told you more than you think. {{title}}

No explanation in this one — just watch. A terminal, and five commands. {{open}} First: who am I. It answers with a name, which is the account these commands run as. {{whoami}} Second: where am I. A path, starting at a slash. That is the current directory, and every command you type will act there unless you say otherwise. {{pwd}} Third: what is here. Four things — three files and a folder. Notice it printed and stopped. No progress bar, no confirmation. {{ls}} Fourth: the same question with one option added, minus l. Same four things, and now a line each: permissions, owner, size, date. The command did not change. What changed is how much of the answer it showed. {{ls-l}} Fifth: show me the inside of that file. Four lines, printed, done. {{cat}} And one more, which is the one worth staying for. I am going to type something that does not exist. {{typo}} There it is. Bash, colon, the thing it could not find, colon, command not found. It looked, it failed, it told me who was speaking and what it was looking for. That is not the machine being unfriendly. That is the most information you will get from any interface you have ever used. {{error}} Five commands and one mistake. The next sections take them apart.
